claims.evidence: This describes the genetic linkage finding, attributed to Schmidt et al.

claims.claim: Chromosome-7 duplication, rather than loss at this location, suggested the involvement of an oncogene suspected of being MET.
claims.source: Chromosome-7 duplication, rather than the loss at this location, suggested the involvement of an oncogene suspected of being MET (Schmidt et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This describes the reasoning that led to suspecting MET as an oncogene, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MET belongs to the same family (the receptor tyrosine kinase family) as RET, a proto-oncogene already known to be mutated in other inherited cancer syndromes.
claims.source: In addition, because MET belongs to the same family (the receptor tyrosine kinase family) as RET, a proto-oncogene already known to be mutated in other inherited cancer syndromes (Cortot et al., 2017), the MET proto-oncogene was sequenced rather than the two other genes also found at this locus.
claims.evidence: This provides context for why MET was prioritized for sequencing, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain.
claims.source: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain, among which germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T) (Schmidt et al., 1997; Schmidt et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes the initial discovery of MET mutations in renal cancer, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Germline MET mutations identified in papillary renal carcinoma include M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C.
claims.source: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain, among which germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T) (Schmidt et al., 1997; Schmidt et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This lists specific germline mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Somatic MET mutations identified in papillary renal carcinoma include D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T.
claims.source: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain, among which germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T) (Schmidt et al., 1997; Schmidt et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This lists specific somatic mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Biochemical and biological assays on murine fibroblasts transfected with MET cDNA demonstrated an increase in MET autophosphorylation when mutations were inserted.
claims.source: Biochemical and biological assays on murine fibroblasts transfected with MET cDNA demonstrated an increase in MET autophosphorylation when mutations were inserted, demonstrating that these are able to cause constitutive activity of the MET receptor (Tovar and Graveel, 2017; Bardelli et al., 1997b; Jeffers et al., 1997; Bardelli et al., 1998; Graveel et al., 2004; Michieli et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes functional assays demonstrating mutation effects, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: MET mutations are able to cause constitutive activity of the MET receptor.
claims.source: Biochemical and biological assays on murine fibroblasts transfected with MET cDNA demonstrated an increase in MET autophosphorylation when mutations were inserted, demonstrating that these are able to cause constitutive activity of the MET receptor (Tovar and Graveel, 2017; Bardelli et al., 1997b; Jeffers et al., 1997; Bardelli et al., 1998; Graveel et al., 2004; Michieli et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from functional assays, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Different levels of tyrosine kinase activity were observed according to the MET mutation.
claims.source: Interestingly, different levels of tyrosine kinase activity were observed according to the mutation (Jeffers et al., 1998)
claims.evidence: This describes variability in mutation effects, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: M1268T substitution is identified as the most active MET mutation, followed by Y1248H, L1213V, and D1246H.
claims.source: M1268T substitutions being identified as the most active, followed by Y1248H, L1213V, and D1246H (Jeffers et al., 1997; Figure 1 and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This ranks mutations by activity level, supported by a citation and Table 1.

claims.claim: Analysis of focus formation, cell motility, and tumour growth in athymic mice demonstrated a correlation between MET enzymatic activity and the transforming properties of the different mutants.
claims.source: Next, analysis of focus formation, cell motility, and tumour growth in athymic mice demonstrated a correlation between MET enzymatic activity and the transforming properties of the different mutants (Bardelli et al., 1997a; Schmidt et al., 1997; Bardelli et al., 1998; Graveel et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes functional studies correlating activity with transformation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: M1268T, the most active mutant, elicited the most marked focus formation.
claims.source: For instance M1268T, the most active mutant, elicited the most marked focus formation (Bardelli et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This provides a specific example of the correlation between activity and transformation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The two most strongly activating MET variants, M1268T and Y1248H, displayed constitutive activity and were found to transform fibroblasts even in the absence of HGF.
claims.source: The two most strongly activating variants, M1268T and Y1248H, displayed constitutive activity, being found to transform fibroblasts even in the absence of HGF (Michieli et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes ligand-independent activity of specific mutations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Other evaluated MET mutations (M1149T, V1206L, L1213V, V1238I), displaying weaker activity, still required HGF stimulation for enhanced MET receptor phosphorylation and cell transformation.
claims.source: In contrast, other evaluated mutations (M1149T, V1206L, L1213V, V1238I), displaying weaker activity, still required HGF stimulation for enhanced MET receptor phosphorylation and cell transformation (Chiara et al., 2003; Michieli et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This describes ligand-dependent activity of specific mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Transformation mediated by MET mutants can depend or not on HGF, according to the initial level of kinase activation.
claims.source: These data suggest that transformation mediated by MET mutants can depend or not on HGF, according to the initial level of kinase activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data on ligand dependence.

claims.claim: Mutations inducing higher MET phosphorylation (M1268T and Y1248H) occur in the C-terminal lobe of the MET receptor, specifically in or above the activation loop.
claims.source: Interestingly, mutations inducing higher MET phosphorylation (M1268T and Y1248H) occur in the C-terminal lobe of the MET receptor, specifically in or above the activation loop (Jeffers et al., 1997)
claims.evidence: This describes the structural location of highly activating mutations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mutations inducing lower phosphorylation (V1206L and M1149T) are located in the N-lobe or near the catalytic site of the kinase domain (between the N and C lobes).
claims.source: while the mutations inducing lower phosphorylation (V1206L and M1149T for instance) are located in the N-lobe or near the catalytic site of the kinase domain (between the N and C lobes).
claims.evidence: This describes the structural location of weakly activating mutations.

claims.claim: There is a relation between mutation location and the activation level of MET.
claims.source: This suggests a relation between mutation location and the activation level.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the structural observations.

claims.claim: Knock-in mouse models for several germline MET mutations demonstrated that these MET mutations can induce spontaneous tumorigenesis.
claims.source: With knock-in mouse models for several germline MET mutations, it has been demonstrated that these MET mutations can induce spontaneous tumorigenesis. This provides strong evidence that activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis (Graveel et al., 2004; Graveel et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This describes in vivo evidence for the oncogenic role of MET mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis.
claims.source: This provides strong evidence that activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis (Graveel et al., 2004; Graveel et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the mouse model studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: For two kinase mutations in the C-terminal lobe, M1268T and Y1248H, an increase in endocytosis/recycling of the receptor to the membrane has been described, along with a decrease in its degradation.
claims.source: For two kinase mutations in the C-terminal lobe, M1268T and Y1248H, an increase in endocytosis/recycling of the receptor to the membrane has been described, along with a decrease in its degradation (Joffre et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes a mechanism of action for specific mutations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In lung cancers, MET mutations mainly affect the juxtamembrane domain, encoded by exon 14.
claims.source: While in renal cancers MET mutations are located exclusively in the kinase domain, in lung cancers they mainly affect the juxtamembrane domain, encoded by exon 14.
claims.evidence: This contrasts the distribution of MET mutations between cancer types.

claims.claim: The first juxtamembrane-domain-located mutations to be discovered were point mutations inducing amino acid substitutions within the domain.
claims.source: The first juxtamembrane-domain-located mutations to be discovered were point mutations inducing amino acid substitutions within the domain (Seiwert et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a historical claim about the discovery of JM domain mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Juxtamembrane domain mutations include R988C, P1009S, and T1010I.
claims.source: These mutations include R988C, P1009S, and T1010I with, for instance, about 1% of NSCLC patients harbouring R988C (Krishnaswamy et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This lists specific JM domain mutations and provides prevalence data, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: About 1% of NSCLC patients harbour the R988C mutation.
claims.source: These mutations include R988C, P1009S, and T1010I with, for instance, about 1% of NSCLC patients harbouring R988C (Krishnaswamy et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This provides prevalence data for R988C in NSCLC, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Amino acid substitutions within the juxtamembrane domain promote migration and colony formation in soft agar and increase levels of reactive oxygen species.
claims.source: Several studies have demonstrated that these amino acid substitutions within the juxtamembrane domain promote migration and colony formation in soft agar and increase levels of reactive oxygen species, a phenomenon liable to participate in cell transformation (Ma, 2015; Jagadeeswaran et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This describes functional effects of JM domain mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Juxtamembrane domain mutations favour the growth of experimental tumours.
claims.source: Furthermore, it has been shown that they favour the growth of experimental tumours.
claims.evidence: This describes in vivo effects of JM domain mutations.

claims.claim: Whether juxtamembrane domain mutations are really activating mutations is controversial, since they do not cause MET kinase activation.
claims.source: Whether these mutations are really activating mutations, however, is controversial, since they do not cause MET kinase activation (Lee et al., 2000; Tyner et al., 2010), so their mode of action is not obvious.
claims.evidence: This acknowledges controversy about the mechanism of JM domain mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Recent studies have shown that juxtamembrane domain mutations can be germline mutations and thus might correspond to polymorphisms.
claims.source: In addition, recent studies have shown that these mutations can be germline mutations and thus might correspond to polymorphisms ( Tyner et al., 2010; Boland et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This suggests an alternative interpretation of JM domain mutations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the murine strain SWRJ, the presence of the R968C MET variant, corresponding to the human R988C variant, favours the development of lung tumours upon exposure to a carcinogen.
claims.source: In the murine strain SWRJ, the presence of the R968C MET variant, corresponding to the human R988C variant, favours the development of lung tumours upon exposure to a carcinogen (Zaffaroni et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This provides in vivo evidence for the functional significance of R988C, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The R988C mutation favours MET proteolytic cleavages by calpain, a cytoplasmic calcium-activated protease.
claims.source: In addition, we have recently demonstrated that the R988C mutation favours MET proteolytic cleavages by calpain, a cytoplasmic calcium-activated protease (Montagne et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes a mechanism of action for R988C, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MET cleavage by calpain leads to the generation of an intracellular fragment of about 45 kDa (p45 MET), which in epithelial cells promotes migration and invasion induced by HGF stimulation.
claims.source: This MET cleavage leads to the generation of an intracellular fragment of about 45 kDa (p45 MET), which in epithelial cells promotes migration and invasion induced by HGF stimulation. This suggests an original mechanism of MET activation, independent of activation of its kinase (Montagne et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the functional consequence of calpain cleavage, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The p45 MET fragment represents an original mechanism of MET activation, independent of activation of its kinase.
claims.source: This suggests an original mechanism of MET activation, independent of activation of its kinase (Montagne et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the p45 MET function, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In contrast to the p40 MET fragment generated during apoptosis, the p45 MET fragment is unable to amplify apoptosis.
claims.source: It is worth noting that, in contrast to the p40 MET fragment generated during apoptosis (see next chapter), the p45 MET fragment is unable to amplify apoptosis. This suggests that differential MET processing by proteases generates specialized fragments according to the cell conditions (Fernandes et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This contrasts two MET fragments and their functions, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Differential MET processing by proteases generates specialized fragments according to the cell conditions.
claims.source: This suggests that differential MET processing by proteases generates specialized fragments according to the cell conditions (Fernandes et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential processing, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Several mutations affecting the splice junctions flanking exon 14 were described in 2006 in two adenocarcinoma tissues and in the NSCLC cell line H596.
claims.source: Besides mutations causing amino-acid substitutions within the juxtamembrane domain, several mutations affecting the splice junctions flanking exon 14, encoding the juxtamembrane domain, were described in 2006 in two adenocarcinoma tissues and in the NSCLC cell line H596 (Kong-Beltran et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a historical claim about the discovery of splice site mutations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In 2014, profiling of lung adenocarcinomas by whole-exome sequencing and mRNA sequencing revealed an approximate 3% rate of somatic mutations leading to exon 14 skipping in lung cancer.
claims.source: In 2014, profiling of lung adenocarcinomas by whole-exome sequencing and mRNA sequencing revealed an approximate 3% rate of somatic mutations leading to exon 14 skipping in lung cancer (Collisson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This provides prevalence data for exon 14 skipping mutations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In 2015, next-generation sequencing (NGS) across several advanced cancers proved the great diversity of MET exon 14 alterations.
claims.source: One year later, the great diversity of MET exon 14 alterations was proved by next-generation sequencing (NGS) across several advanced cancers, including lung, gastric, colorectal, and brain cancers (Frampton et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the discovery of diversity in exon 14 alterations, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: At the 5' end of exon 14, most of the alterations are deletions, insertions, and indels affecting the acceptor splice site, the branch point, or the polypyrimidine tract.
claims.source: At the 5' end of the exon, most of the alterations are deletions, insertions, and indels affecting the acceptor splice site, the branch point, or the polypyrimidine tract.
claims.evidence: This describes the types of alterations at the 5' end of exon 14.

claims.claim: At the 3' end of exon 14, alterations are mostly point mutations affecting the donor splice site.
claims.source: At the 3' end, they are mostly point mutations affecting the donor splice site (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This describes the types of alterations at the 3' end of exon 14, supported by Figure 2A.

claims.claim: All exon 14 alterations potentially lead to in-phase exon 14 skipping, as demonstrated by RNA sequencing.
claims.source: Interestingly, all these alterations potentially lead to in-phase exon 14 skipping, as demonstrated by RNA sequencing (Kong-Beltran et al., 2006; Collisson et al., 2014; Davies et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the consequence of the alterations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In normal mouse liver and kidney, alternative splicing affecting exon 15 (corresponding to exon 14 in human) has been described.
claims.source: In normal mouse liver and kidney, alternative splicing affecting exon 15 (corresponding to exon 14 in human) has been described (exon 15 in transcript ID ENSMUST00000115443).
claims.evidence: This describes a natural alternative splicing event in mice.

claims.claim: Alternative splicing of mouse exon 15 induces a 141-basepair deletion predicted to result in a 47-amino-acid in-frame deletion in the juxtamembrane region of the cytoplasmic part.
claims.source: It has been proved that this rare alternative splicing event induces a 141-basepair deletion predicted to result in a 47-amino-acid in-frame deletion in the juxtamembrane region of the cytoplasmic part (Lee and Yamada, 1994).
claims.evidence: This describes the molecular consequence of the alternative splicing, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mouse fibroblasts expressing the MET variant with exon 15 deletion display transforming phenotypes and form tumours in immunodeficient mice.
claims.source: This rare alternative splicing event has not been described, to date, in normal human tissues, but mouse fibroblasts expressing the MET variant with the described deletion display transforming phenotypes and form tumours in immunodeficient mice. This suggests that deletion of exon 15 (corresponding to exon 14 in human) may promote tumorigenesis (Lee et al., 2006; Baek et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes functional evidence for the oncogenic potential of exon deletion, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Deletion of exon 15 in mouse (corresponding to exon 14 in human) may promote tumorigenesis.
claims.source: This suggests that deletion of exon 15 (corresponding to exon 14 in human) may promote tumorigenesis (Lee et al., 2006; Baek et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the mouse model data, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the exon-14-encoded juxtamembrane domain of human MET, several negative regulatory sites have been characterized.
claims.source: More recently, in the exon-14-encoded juxtamembrane domain of human MET, several negative regulatory sites have been characterized.
claims.evidence: This introduces the characterization of regulatory sites in the JM domain.

claims.claim: Serine 1003 (Ser985 in the short MET isoform) is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC) and dephosphorylated by protein phosphatase 2 A (PP2A).
claims.source: The first negative regulatory mechanism found to target the juxtamembrane region was phosphorylation of serine 1003 (Ser985 in the short MET isoform). Ser1003 is phosphorylated by protein kinase C (PKC) and dephosphorylated by protein phosphatase 2 A (PP2A) (Hashigasako et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the regulation of Ser1003, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of MET Ser1003 impairs proper phosphorylation of tyrosine residues, and can thus control cell responsiveness to HGF.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of MET Ser1003 impairs proper phosphorylation of tyrosine residues, and can thus control cell responsiveness to HGF (Gandino et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This describes the functional consequence of Ser1003 phosphorylation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: After liver injury, ligand-dependent activation of the MET kinase, required for tissue regeneration, correlates with decreased Ser1003 phosphorylation.
claims.source: After liver injury, it has been proved that ligand-dependent activation of the MET kinase, required for tissue regeneration, correlates with decreased Ser1003 phosphorylation (Nakayama et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes the physiological role of Ser1003 regulation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Deletion of exon 14 could confer insensitivity to MET-inhibiting signals conveyed by PKC, thus leading to MET activation.
claims.source: On this basis it would seem that deletion of exon 14 could confer insensitivity to MET-inhibiting signals conveyed by PKC, thus leading to MET activation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the consequence of exon 14 deletion.

claims.claim: Following MET activation, the phosphorylated Tyr1021 residue participates in MET ubiquitination by recruiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL to the DYpR motif.
claims.source: Following MET activation, the phosphorylated Tyr1021 residue participates in MET ubiquitination by recruiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL (Casitas B-lineage lymphoma) to the DYpR motif, through interaction with the tyrosine kinase binding domain (TKB) (Peschard et al., 2001; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanism of CBL recruitment, supported by a citation and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Tyr1021 mutation does not impair clathrin-dependent MET internalisation although, if the mutant is internalized, the absence of ubiquitination could prevent its efficient degradation.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Tyr1021 mutation does not impair clathrin-dependent MET internalisation although, if the mutant is internalized, the absence of ubiquitination could prevent its efficient degradation (Li et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This describes the effect of Tyr1021 mutation on MET trafficking, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MET mutated at Tyr1021 promotes more marked cell motility and displays higher stability and a greater transforming capacity than the wild-type version.
claims.source: It has been demonstrated that MET mutated at Tyr1021 promotes more marked cell motility and displays higher stability and a greater transforming capacity than the wild-type version (Weidner et al., 1995; Lai et al., 2012; Abella et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This describes the functional consequences of Tyr1021 mutation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Upon stress induction and in the absence of ligand, the MET receptor is first cleaved at a consensus caspase site in its C-terminal tail, followed by a second cleavage at aspartic acid 1020 (Asp1020) within an ESVD motif of the juxtamembrane domain.
claims.source: Upon stress induction and in the absence of ligand, the MET receptor is first cleaved at a consensus caspase site in its C-terminal tail. This initial cleavage is followed by a second one, at aspartic acid 1020 (Asp1020) within an ESVD motif of the juxtamembrane domain. This leads to the generation of a 40 kDa cytoplasmic C-terminal fragment (p40 MET) containing the tyrosine kinase domain (Figure 2B; Foveau et al., 2007; Tulasne et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the caspase cleavage mechanism, supported by citations and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Caspase cleavages of MET lead to the generation of a 40 kDa cytoplasmic C-terminal fragment (p40 MET) containing the tyrosine kinase domain.
claims.source: This leads to the generation of a 40 kDa cytoplasmic C-terminal fragment (p40 MET) containing the tyrosine kinase domain (Figure 2B; Foveau et al., 2007; Tulasne et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This describes the product of caspase cleavage, supported by citations and Figure 2B.

claims.claim: During apoptosis, the level of full-length MET receptor decreases drastically after the caspase cleavages.
claims.source: During apoptosis, the level of full-length MET receptor decreases drastically after the caspase cleavages.
claims.evidence: This describes the consequence of caspase cleavage on MET levels.

claims.claim: The separation of the extracellular ligand-binding domain from the kinase domain prevents receptor activation by its ligand.
claims.source: Furthermore, the separation of the extracellular ligand-binding domain from the kinase domain prevents receptor activation by its ligand.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequence of cleavage.

claims.claim: Caspase cleavages convert MET to a pro-apoptotic fragment (p40 MET) capable of stimulating cell death, by promoting calcium flux involved in mitochondrial permeabilization.
claims.source: Beside the fact that caspase cleavages inactivate the receptor, they also convert it to a pro-apoptotic fragment (p40 MET) capable of stimulating cell death, by promoting calcium flux involved in mitochondrial permeabilization (Lefebvre et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This describes the pro-apoptotic function of p40 MET, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In knock-in mice expressing a MET variant mutated at the C-terminal caspase cleavage site, production of a functional p40 MET is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, in knock-in mice expressing a MET variant mutated at the C-terminal caspase cleavage site, we have highlighted that production of a functional p40 MET is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis. Thus, MET acts in vivo as a dependence receptor, through an original signalling mechanism controlling mitochondrial permeabilization (Duplaquet et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes in vivo evidence for the role of p40 MET in apoptosis, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MET acts in vivo as a dependence receptor, through an original signalling mechanism controlling mitochondrial permeabilization.
claims.source: Thus, MET acts in vivo as a dependence receptor, through an original signalling mechanism controlling mitochondrial permeabilization (Duplaquet et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about MET's role as a dependence receptor, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ESVD1020 caspase cleavage site overlaps with the DYp1021R recruitment motif for CBL, and phosphorylation of Y1021 prevents caspase cleavage.
claims.source: Interestingly, the ESVD1020 caspase cleavage site overlaps with the DYp1021R recruitment motif for CBL (ESVD1020Yp1021R), and phosphorylation of Y1021 prevents caspase cleavage. This suggests a mechanism protecting phosphorylated MET against caspase cleavage (Deheuninck et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This describes the relationship between phosphorylation and caspase cleavage, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of Y1021 suggests a mechanism protecting phosphorylated MET against caspase cleavage.
claims.source: This suggests a mechanism protecting phosphorylated MET against caspase cleavage (Deheuninck et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the protective role of phosphorylation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Activation of the METex14Del variant still depends on ligand stimulation.
claims.source: It appears, firstly, that activation of the METex14Del variant still depends on ligand stimulation.
claims.evidence: This describes a key property of the METex14Del variant.

claims.claim: METex14Del induces stronger and more sustained activation of receptor kinase activity and downstream signalling pathways, including the RAS signalling pathway.
claims.source: Second, METex14Del induces stronger and more sustained activation of receptor kinase activity and downstream signalling pathways, including the RAS signalling pathway, resulting in significant activation of cell responses such as migration, scattering, and invasion in vitro and metastasis in vivo (Kong-Beltran et al., 2006; Fernandes et al., 2023a; Togashi et al., 2015; Frampton et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This describes the functional consequences of METex14Del, supported by citations.

claims.claim: METex14Del results in significant activation of cell responses such as migration, scattering, and invasion in vitro and metastasis in vivo.
claims.source: Second, METex14Del induces stronger and more sustained activation of receptor kinase activity and downstream signalling pathways, including the RAS signalling pathway, resulting in significant activation of cell responses such as migration, scattering, and invasion in vitro and metastasis in vivo (Kong-Beltran et al., 2006; Fernandes et al., 2023a; Togashi et al., 2015; Frampton et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This describes the biological consequences of METex14Del, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Transcriptomic analyses after HGF stimulation revealed expression of matrix metalloproteases known to promote motility and invasion and to be regulated by the RAS signalling pathway.
claims.source: Transcriptomic analyses after HGF stimulation have notably revealed expression of matrix metalloproteases known to promote motility and invasion (Cabral-Pacheco et al., 2020) and to be regulated by the RAS signalling pathway (Yang et al., 2014; Tanimura et al., 2003; Genersch et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This describes transcriptomic findings, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sustained activation of RAS-ERK signalling by the METex14Del variant induces expression of MMPs promoting cell motility and invasion.
claims.source: This suggests that sustained activation of RAS-ERK signalling by the METex14Del variant induces expression of MMPs promoting cell motility and invasion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the transcriptomic data.

claims.claim: The CBL binding site, involved in MET ubiquitination, is a crucial regulatory site in the juxtamembrane domain.
claims.source: Only a few functional studies have explored the respective roles of the three known regulatory sites of the juxtamembrane domain in regulating receptor and downstream signalling pathway activation. It seems, however, that the CBL binding site, involved in MET ubiquitination, is a crucial regulatory site (Fernandes et al., 2023b; Miao and Xu, 2019).
claims.evidence: This identifies the most important regulatory site, supported by citations.

claims.claim: When METex14Del is present, other known oncogenic drivers such as KRAS, EGFR, and HER2 tend to be absent.
claims.source: Furthermore, when METex14Del is present, other known oncogenic drivers such as KRAS (Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog), EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor), and HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) tend to be absent, which suggests that METex14Del can promote oncogenesis in the absence of other oncogenic drivers (Pilotto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the mutual exclusivity of METex14Del with other drivers, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: METex14Del can promote oncogenesis in the absence of other oncogenic drivers.
claims.source: which suggests that METex14Del can promote oncogenesis in the absence of other oncogenic drivers (Pilotto et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the mutual exclusivity data, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Previously untreated patients displaying MET dysregulation in NSCLC (due to MET exon 14 skipping, MET amplification, or both) display bad prognosis.
claims.source: The prognostic impact of MET exon 14 skipping has not yet been studied extensively, but previously untreated patients displaying MET dysregulation in NSCLC (due to MET exon 14 skipping, MET amplification, or both) display bad prognosis (Awad, 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the prognostic significance of MET dysregulation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MET exon 14 skipping alterations are associated, in patients with NSCLC, with poorer outcome.
claims.source: These results constitute evidence that MET exon 14 skipping alterations are associated, in patients with NSCLC, with poorer outcome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the prognostic impact of exon 14 skipping.

claims.claim: MET N375S, the most common polymorphism known to affect the MET gene, causes an amino acid substitution in the semaphorin domain and is found in several cancers, including lung cancers.
claims.source: Yet MET N375S, the most common polymorphism known to affect the MET gene and which causes an amino acid substitution in the semaphorin domain, is found also in several cancers, including lung cancers (Tengs et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This describes a common MET polymorphism and its cancer association, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: METN375S can confer exquisite binding affinity for HER2, enabling METN375S to interact with HER2 in a ligand-independent fashion.
claims.source: Interestingly, this mutation can confer exquisite binding affinity for HER2, enabling METN375S to interact with HER2 in a ligand-independent fashion. The resulting METN375S/HER2 dimer transduces potent proliferative, pro-invasive, and pro-metastatic cues through the HER2 signaling axis to drive aggressive HNSCC and LUSC cancers (Kong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This describes a novel mechanism of action for N375S, supported by a citation.

results.result: The first MET mutation was discovered in 1997 in hereditary papillary renal cancer (HPRC) through genomic polymorphism analysis by Schmidt et al., establishing the first direct link between MET mutations and cancer development. The disease was found to segregate with a locus on chromosome 7q carrying the MET proto-oncogene, and chromosome-7 duplication suggested oncogene involvement. Analysis of nine families identified germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, M1268T) in the kinase domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C49-C56 collectively establish the historical discovery of MET mutations in HPRC with specific dates, genetic linkage data, and identified mutations. The claims are well-supported by citations to Schmidt et al. (1997, 1999) and provide converging evidence from genetic linkage analysis and mutation identification in multiple families.

results.result: Functional characterization of MET kinase domain mutations demonstrated that they cause constitutive MET receptor activity with varying levels of tyrosine kinase activation. M1268T was identified as the most active mutation, followed by Y1248H, L1213V, and D1246H. The most strongly activating variants (M1268T and Y1248H) displayed ligand-independent transformation, while weaker mutations (M1149T, V1206L, L1213V, V1238I) required HGF stimulation. A correlation was observed between mutation location (C-terminal lobe vs. N-lobe) and activation level.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C68 provide comprehensive functional characterization data from multiple assays (autophosphorylation, focus formation, cell motility, tumor growth) supported by numerous citations. The data consistently demonstrate varying levels of activation and establish structure-function relationships, though the mechanistic basis for location-dependent effects could be more thoroughly explored.

results.result: Knock-in mouse models for several germline MET mutations demonstrated that these mutations can induce spontaneous tumorigenesis, providing strong in vivo evidence that activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 describe definitive in vivo evidence from knock-in mouse models, supported by citations to Graveel et al. (2004, 2005). This represents the gold standard for demonstrating oncogenic potential, though the claims would be strengthened by specifying which mutations were tested and the tumor types observed.

results.result: Novel MET mutations affecting exon 14 splice sites were identified starting in 2006, with comprehensive characterization in 2014 revealing approximately 3% prevalence in lung cancer. More than 160 different alterations have been described, including point mutations, deletions, insertions, and indels affecting conserved splice site sequences at both the 5' and 3' ends of exon 14. All alterations lead to in-phase exon 14 skipping and deletion of the juxtamembrane regulatory domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C44, C86-C91 document the discovery and characterization of exon 14 mutations with specific dates, prevalence data, and molecular details supported by multiple citations. The progression from initial discovery to comprehensive NGS-based characterization is well-documented, though C8 acknowledges that the mode of action remains incompletely understood.

results.result: The exon 14-encoded juxtamembrane domain contains three characterized negative regulatory sites: (1) Ser1003, phosphorylated by PKC, which impairs tyrosine phosphorylation and controls HGF responsiveness; (2) Tyr1021, which recruits CBL E3 ubiquitin ligase for receptor ubiquitination and degradation; and (3) Asp1020, a caspase cleavage site that generates the pro-apoptotic p40 MET fragment. These sites overlap (ESVD1020Yp1021R), with Y1021 phosphorylation protecting against caspase cleavage. Knock-in mouse studies confirmed that p40 MET production is important for FAS-driven hepatocyte apoptosis, establishing MET as a dependence receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C112 provide detailed molecular characterization of three regulatory mechanisms in the juxtamembrane domain, supported by multiple citations and in vivo validation. The overlapping nature of the regulatory sites and their functional consequences are well-documented, with particularly strong evidence from knock-in mouse models (C109-C110) for the apoptotic function.

results.result: The METex14Del variant, while still requiring ligand stimulation, induces stronger and more sustained activation of receptor kinase activity and downstream signaling pathways, particularly RAS-ERK signaling. This results in significant activation of migration, scattering, invasion in vitro and metastasis in vivo. Transcriptomic analyses revealed expression of matrix metalloproteases regulated by RAS signaling. The CBL binding site appears to be the most crucial regulatory site among the three in the juxtamembrane domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C118 characterize the functional consequences of exon 14 deletion with data from multiple cell models (HEK293, H292, 16HBE) and tumor cell lines, supported by citations. The ligand dependence (C113) and sustained signaling (C114-C115) are well-documented, though C118's conclusion about CBL being the most crucial site is based on limited comparative functional studies as acknowledged in the text.

results.result: METex14Del displays mutual exclusivity with other oncogenic drivers (KRAS, EGFR, HER2), suggesting it can promote oncogenesis independently. Previously untreated NSCLC patients with MET dysregulation (exon 14 skipping, amplification, or both) display poor prognosis, providing evidence that MET exon 14 skipping alterations are associated with poorer outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 establish the driver status and prognostic significance of METex14Del, supported by citations. The mutual exclusivity data (C119) strongly suggests driver function, though C121 acknowledges limited study of prognostic impact specifically for exon 14 skipping alone (as opposed to combined MET dysregulation).

results.result: Multiple clinical trials demonstrated efficacy of MET TKIs in papillary renal cell carcinoma (PRCC) patients with MET mutations. Foretinib showed 50% response rate in germline MET mutation patients with manageable toxicity. Savolitinib showed numerically superior response rate to sunitinib (27% vs 7%) in the SAVOIR trial. Crizotinib demonstrated >1 year progression-free survival with 75% disease control in the CREATE trial. Combination of savolitinib with durvalumab showed 12-month median PFS and 27.4-month OS in MET-impaired metastatic RCC.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C134 present clinical trial data for MET TKI efficacy in PRCC, supported by citations. The mutation-specific responses (C127-C129) provide strong evidence for targeted therapy efficacy. However, C131 notes the SAVOIR trial was prematurely terminated, and sample sizes are relatively small, limiting the strength of conclusions.

results.result: Preclinical and clinical studies demonstrated efficacy of MET TKIs in NSCLC patients with MET exon 14 skipping. Crizotinib showed efficacy in case studies and a trial of 69 patients (9.1-month median response duration, 7.3-month median PFS), leading to FDA breakthrough therapy designation in May 2018. Tepotinib induced 50% objective response (11-month response duration, 17.1-month OS) in the VISION trial, leading to Japanese approval. Capmatinib showed objective responses (12.6-month median response duration) in the GEOMETRY trial, leading to FDA approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C145 document the translation from preclinical studies to regulatory approval, supported by multiple citations and specific trial data. The progression from case studies to larger trials and regulatory approvals is well-documented. However, the relatively short response durations and PFS suggest limited durability, and C146 notes that resistance systematically develops.

results.result: Resistance to MET TKIs systematically develops after initial responses, with both off-target (other RTKs, downstream signaling) and on-target mechanisms. On-target resistance involves mutations in the MET kinase domain at positions H1112, G1181, L1213, F1218, D1246, and Y1248, typically emerging within months of treatment. Multiple mutations can co-occur (e.g., D1246N/H with Y1248H; G1181R with L1213V, D1246H/N, Y1248H/S). Among 20 patients with resistance, 35% displayed on-target MET mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C154 comprehensively document resistance mechanisms with specific mutations, timing, and prevalence data supported by numerous citations. The identification of multiple co-occurring mutations (C151-C153) and quantification of on-target vs off-target resistance (C154) provide strong evidence, though the relatively small patient numbers limit generalizability.

results.result: Most resistance mutations were previously identified as activating mutations in renal cancer, suggesting they confer ligand-independent MET activation. Cell model studies revealed 12 resistance mutations, with type I TKI resistance associated with mutations at positions 1246 and 1248, and type II TKI resistance with mutations at 1213 and 1218. Structural analysis shows these mutations cause steric hindrance of TKI binding. MET variants with resistance to one TKI type appear sensitive to the other type, suggesting resistance might be overcome through complementary TKI activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C164 connect resistance mutations to known activating mutations and provide mechanistic insights from cell models and structural analysis, supported by citations. The TKI type-specific resistance patterns (C158-C160) and structural basis (C161-C162) are well-documented. The suggestion of complementary TKI activity (C163-C164) is supported by cell model data but requires clinical validation.

results.result: A clinical case demonstrated that switching from type I TKI (crizotinib) to type II TKI (glesatinib) in a patient with MET exon 14 skipping and resistance mutations (D1246N, Y1248H/S, G1181R) led to regression of metastases with disappearance of Y1248H/S mutation, but concomitant appearance of L1213V mutation (associated with type II TKI resistance).
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C168 provide clinical validation of the TKI type-switching strategy with detailed mutation tracking, supported by citation to Engstrom et al. (2017). The case demonstrates both the potential and limitations of this approach, as new resistance emerged. However, this is a single case report, limiting generalizability.

results.result: A patient with EGFR-activating mutation developed MET amplification-mediated resistance to EGFR TKI. Co-treatment with EGFR TKI and MET TKI savolitinib produced dramatic response, but relapse occurred with D1246V mutation. Cell line studies showed D1246V confers resistance to type I TKIs but not type II inhibitors. Switching to EGFR TKI plus cabozantinib (type II MET TKI) produced very good response.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C172 document a clinically important case of MET-mediated EGFR TKI resistance and successful treatment adaptation based on functional characterization, supported by citation to Bahcall et al. (2016). The integration of cell model data to guide treatment switching demonstrates translational value, though this is a single case.

results.result: In patients with MET gene amplification treated with various TKIs, resistance mutations at D1246 and Y1248 emerged, similar to those found in exon 14 skipping context, suggesting main on-target resistances are common between wild-type MET and METex14Del variant.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C174 extend resistance mutation findings to MET amplification context and draw an important inference about shared resistance mechanisms, supported by citation to Yao et al. (2023). The observation of similar mutations across different MET activation mechanisms strengthens the conclusion, though more systematic comparison would be valuable.

results.result: In lung cancers, MET mutations mainly affect the juxtamembrane domain (exon 14), contrasting with renal cancers. Point mutations (R988C, P1009S, T1010I) were first discovered, with R988C found in ~1% of NSCLC patients. These mutations promote migration, colony formation, and ROS production, and favor experimental tumor growth. However, their classification as activating mutations is controversial since they don't cause kinase activation. R988C favors calpain-mediated cleavage generating p45 MET fragment, which promotes HGF-induced migration/invasion independent of kinase activation. This represents a novel, kinase-independent mechanism distinct from the apoptotic p40 MET fragment.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C85 describe juxtamembrane domain mutations with functional data, but C78-C79 explicitly acknowledge controversy about whether these are true activating mutations and suggest they might be polymorphisms. While C80-C83 provide mechanistic data for R988C through calpain cleavage, the overall oncogenic role remains uncertain. The distinction from p40 MET (C84) is well-supported, but the functional significance of p45 MET requires further validation.

results.result: In normal mouse liver and kidney, alternative splicing of exon 15 (corresponding to human exon 14) has been described, resulting in a 141-bp deletion and 47-amino-acid in-frame deletion in the juxtamembrane region. Mouse fibroblasts expressing this MET variant display transforming phenotypes and form tumors in immunodeficient mice, suggesting exon deletion may promote tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 provide evidence from mouse models that exon 14 deletion can be oncogenic, supported by citations to Lee et al. (2006) and Baek et al. (2004). The functional data from mouse fibroblasts and tumor formation studies support the oncogenic potential, though the text notes this alternative splicing has not been described in normal human tissues.

results.result: For two kinase mutations in the C-terminal lobe (M1268T and Y1248H), increased endocytosis/recycling to the membrane and decreased degradation have been described.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 describes a specific mechanism for two highly activating mutations, supported by citation to Joffre et al. (2011). This provides mechanistic insight into how these mutations maintain high receptor levels, though the text notes that downstream signaling has been little investigated for most mutations.

results.result: MET N375S, the most common MET polymorphism causing amino acid substitution in the semaphorin domain, is found in several cancers including lung cancers. This mutation confers binding affinity for HER2, enabling ligand-independent METN375S/HER2 interaction that transduces proliferative, pro-invasive, and pro-metastatic signals through HER2 signaling to drive aggressive HNSCC and LUSC cancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125 describe a novel mechanism for an extracellular domain mutation, supported by citation to Kong et al. (2020). The ligand-independent HER2 interaction represents an unexpected mechanism distinct from typical MET activation, with functional consequences well-documented. This challenges the view of N375S as a benign polymorphism.

results.result: MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed mainly in epithelial cells and activated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). MET/HGF activation promotes invasive growth (cell division, motility, ECM digestion, invasion, survival, morphogenic differentiation) and is involved in embryonic development, organ/tissue development (placenta, liver, lung, muscle), and tissue regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C17 provide well-established background on MET biology, supported by multiple citations. These are foundational facts about MET function and expression that provide context for understanding mutations, but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this work.

results.result: MET is synthesized as a precursor that undergoes proteolytic cleavage to form a heterodimeric receptor with defined extracellular (SEMA, PSI, four IPT domains) and intracellular (juxtamembrane, tyrosine kinase, C-terminal tail) domains. HGF is a 90 kDa heterodimeric protein with α subunit (N domain, k1-k4 loop domains) and β chain (SPH domain lacking catalytic activity). HGF/MET interaction involves SPH and k1 binding to SEMA domain, with two proposed dimerization models (2:2 symmetric and 2:1 asymmetric). Upon activation, MET undergoes phosphorylation at Y1252/Y1253 in the catalytic domain, then at Y1367/Y1374 in the C-terminal multisubstrate docking site, which recruits multiple effectors (GAB1, GRB2, SHC, PI3K, SRC, STAT3, PLCγ) to induce signaling pathways and biological responses. The juxtamembrane region (exon 14, Tyr1021) provides negative regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C30 provide comprehensive structural and mechanistic background on MET receptor biology, supported by multiple citations and Figure 1. These represent well-established prior knowledge that provides essential context for understanding mutations, but are not novel findings from this work.

results.result: Four main genomic mechanisms activate MET in cancer: (1) gene amplification/copy number gain leading to overexpression and ligand-independent activation in glioblastoma, LUAD, gastric, colorectal cancers, and medulloblastoma (first observed in gastric carcinoma); (2) HGF overexpression establishing autocrine loops in breast, gastric, colon, and lung cancers; (3) chromosomal rearrangements creating MET fusions (KIF5B-MET in LUAD; BAIAP2L1-MET and C8ORF34-MET in RCC) causing constitutive activation; and (4) activating mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C40 comprehensively catalog MET activation mechanisms in cancer, supported by multiple citations. This provides important context for understanding the relative importance of mutations versus other mechanisms, representing well-established prior knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: The majority of MET mutations were found in papillary renal cancer in the tyrosine kinase domain. Over the last decade, mutations have been identified outside the kinase domain, including in NSCLC where missense mutations in SEMA and JM domains occur in addition to exon 14 skipping mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 summarize the distribution of MET mutations across cancer types and domains, supported by citations and Figure 1/Table 1. This provides important context but represents a summary of prior discoveries rather than novel findings.

results.result: Renal cell carcinoma is the most common kidney cancer in adults, with clear cell RCC accounting for 80% and papillary RCC (15-20%) being the most common non-clear cell subtype. PRCC is divided into type I and II (distinguished histologically, type II being hereditary).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide epidemiological and classification background on renal cancers, supported by citations. This is standard medical knowledge providing context for understanding HPRC, but represents background rather than novel findings.

results.result: MET mutations are classified as drivers based on functional demonstration of cell transformation and/or tumor growth. Several dozen residues are affected by activating substitutions. Kinase domain mutations (mainly in renal cancers) lead to kinase activation and downstream pathway induction. In contrast, the vast majority of lung cancer mutations (~160 different) cause exon 14 skipping. This differential distribution suggests specific organ contexts favor specific transformation mechanisms. METex14Del induces sustained RAS-ERK signaling (activated in lung cancer) and confers apoptosis resistance through loss of caspase site, potentially favoring lung tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C181 synthesize observations about mutation distribution and propose organ-specific mechanisms, supported by data presented throughout the manuscript. The inference about organ context (C179) is reasonable but speculative. C181 appropriately uses cautious language ('could favour') for the mechanistic speculation.

results.result: The METex14Del variant requires HGF stimulation despite being an activating mutation. Similarly, most kinase-domain-mutated MET forms in renal cancers can be further stimulated by HGF (except M1268T). This suggests RTKs with activating mutations may still require ligand stimulation, and HGF expression by tumor cells or microenvironment could be an attractive biomarker for predicting MET activation and TKI sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C184 document ligand dependence of 'activating' mutations with citation support, challenging the assumption that activating mutations are ligand-independent. C185's biomarker proposal is speculative but logically follows from the ligand dependence data. This represents an important conceptual insight with potential clinical implications.

results.result: Treatment with MET TKIs has led to identifying novel resistance mutations located near the MET-TKI interface that inhibit TKI binding. Some resistance mutations were previously identified in hereditary/sporadic renal cancer. With extensive high-throughput sequencing and targeted therapy use, novel MET mutations are constantly being discovered. The challenge is no longer identification but functional characterization to: (1) identify therapeutic targets, (2) adapt treatment for resistance, (3) understand cancer type-specific mutation patterns, and (4) identify novel biomarkers.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C191 synthesize the current state and future challenges in the field, supported by citations and structural data (Figure 3B). C189 connects new resistance mutations to historical activating mutations. C191 appropriately identifies functional characterization as the key challenge, though this is more of a perspective than a testable result.

results.result: MET TKIs have been recently approved for advanced NSCLC with activating MET mutations. Less than five years after discovering exon 14 skipping mutations, MET TKI efficacy was demonstrated in NSCLC patients, but use led to resistance involving acquisition of novel and previously characterized MET mutations. Novel somatic MET mutations are constantly being discovered.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C11 provide high-level summary of the clinical translation and ongoing discovery, supported by the detailed evidence presented in other claim groups. These represent accurate summary statements of the field's progress and current state.

results.result: MET mutations in the kinase domain lead in most cases to ligand-independent MET activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C4 states that kinase domain mutations lead 'in most cases' to ligand-independent activation, but this is contradicted by later claims (C64, C184) showing that most kinase-domain mutations (except M1268T) still require or benefit from HGF stimulation. The claim oversimplifies the ligand dependence of these mutations.
